content:
On 9 August this year, the Hong Kong Observatory recorded the highest temperature of 36.9°C since records began in 1884, while Sheung Shui hit an even higher 39.8°C in the mid-afternoon. In the sweltering heat, I hid in a long, narrow flat, leaving only a crack in the window for air. In extreme heat, the hot air really does rush indoors. So I shut the balcony door and the living room window completely. I live on the middle floor of a building nestled between two small hills, and apart from noon, the sun is blocked from all sides. Even without air conditioning, three ceiling fans whirred and creaked, spinning cool breezes through the flat. In Hong Kong's heatwaves, one has to be grateful.

During the hottest weather on record, I stayed home and did laundry. Shortly after 1pm, I washed two large bedsheets and duvet covers, four pairs of jeans, and a pile of T-shirts. Two hours later, I turned the sheets and covers over to sun-dry on the other side. After 6pm, I gathered the warm cloth, just as if taking it out of a large washing machine at a laundry shop, and laid it on the bed. It felt as if I had not experienced such naturally sun-dried, clean laundry for half a century. I should have been worrying about my friends under the fierce sun, but only by washing the clothes one load at a time could I offset the awfulness of the blazing sun, even just a little.

August has become a nightmare. I do not know how many more times it will take to shake off that repeated summer of partings. In a dream one night, I strutted proudly, holding my mother by the arm as we walked, saying: "My little mummy." Gripping her tightly in my joy. Then, I saw ahead a mysterious woman draped in a long, deep maroon cloak. My subconscious did not want to see her face clearly, but in the end, the camera in the dream kept zooming into her face—she was a strange woman I did not recognise. Until I woke, a feeling of ecstatic abandon welled up, and what I remembered was: I had dreamed of my mother again.

On the evening of 10 August 2020, our family sang hymns, kissed my mother's forehead, and bade her farewell. It was a full stop. Yet learning to let go is a lesson hard to master in a lifetime. The unwillingness to part is a quiet wound. Six years on, there are still thousands of small regrets in the little details, my mind repeatedly re-enacting the days that led to that moment six years ago.

The regret and reluctance of parting come sooner or later, regardless of age, appearing at different stages of life. A student in my writing class wrote about her grandmother who had passed away. It was a piece of remembrance, mourning, or regret. When she was even younger, she had despised living with her grandmother in the countryside. During the day, with the vigour of a little monster, she would bicker with her grandmother. Her grandmother would pinch her ear, and she would hit back, letting her grandmother feel the pain she had felt. Then, through a crack in the door, the little girl saw her frail, ailing grandmother secretly wiping away tears. That night, the girl fell ill with a fever, and wandered blankly to her grandmother, saying: "I feel unwell."

Unwell means uncomfortable—it is how a child feels sickness. She burned with a high fever, and her grandmother, without a word, found fresh clothes for her to change into, then immediately carried her on her back to the hospital to wait to see the doctor. The smell of medicated oil, once despised, now vaguely accompanied her to the hospital. Before long, somehow, that scent of medicated oil vanished, and the little girl sat alone near the reception desk waiting. Then, some adults asked her: "Where are your family?" As she spoke, she began to cry, until the smell of medicated oil drifted close again, and she felt at peace, waiting properly for the doctor to give her an injection and medicine.

Back home, the smell of medicated oil was as usual, but seemed to have lost its sharpness. From the kitchen came the sound of meat being chopped on the cutting board, and the fragrance of rice porridge wafting from the hot pot. The essence of life in this world needs no further explanation—it is simply this clear and plain.

I wonder, who is it that cooks congee for me when I am sick today?

When I was young, it was mostly my father, sometimes my mother, who would patiently hand-chop beef to make congee for me. This was my sick-day menu, and only I was allowed to eat it. Sometimes, after seeing the doctor, I would pre-order this kind of minced beef congee: "I want scallion and beef congee." It was a sick-day privilege. Now, no one makes this particular congee for me anymore. When I am ill, I will no longer eat this kind of beef congee.

"If you're sick now, just order from Foodpanda," a friend said. Other friends cook plain congee or fish congee for their wives. "Sometimes I make minced pork congee too." "Hand-chopping, not using a blender." "It's done in a few minutes." Because of a pot of congee, one feels cherished.

"In a lifetime, not many people will cook congee for you when you are sick. After growing up, the most likely scenario is that you cook it for others. Many people have gone through this. Whatever your feelings may be, say a proper goodbye, speak from the heart. Those who read it will feel comforted for you." I said to the student. She looked at me, a glint of light flashing in her eyes.

A piece of writing about one's grandmother can bring comfort. My father, my mother, my grandmother... these are stories we naturally know how to write.

The student's strength is not simply good prose. She seized upon the medicated oil as the central thread, weaving around it to express her true feelings about her closest relative. She may not have loved her grandmother the most, but that time together, arranged by fate, means she cannot forget everything her grandmother did for her today, nor fail to understand that people grow up in ways they themselves do not fully grasp. In the end, she submitted a piece that was deeply moving and, indeed, "unwell"-inducing.

Medicated oil transformed from being detested, to reliable, to shameful, to a memory to be cherished. It turns out that on the first day the student started primary school, classmates laughed at her for smelling of medicated oil, calling her a country bumpkin. She ran home crying, and forcefully commanded her grandmother to wash all the clothes from top to bottom with heavy doses of detergent. Grandmother held the clothes and cried. From when the girl was eight months old, grandmother had raised her until she grew up and went to school. After being exposed to the outside world, the granddaughter seemed to become a different person, and she hurt her grandmother's heart. After returning to live with her mother, one day grandmother had already developed dementia (Alzheimer's disease). The student went back with her mother to visit the elderly woman, and found that she was no longer "recognised".

"You can't be my granddaughter—she didn't like talking to me," the old grandmother said to the student.

Life is both real and cruel. Have I ever been this cruel to my mother? It seems not. Or perhaps I have, and like the student, I simply do not know. Family members sometimes hurt one another. The point is, going forward, have we come to understand love more deeply?
